title: continuous-batcher: scheduler tuning for queueing fairness, starvation prevention, and adaptive timeouts
author: Liam Chen
description:
Motivation: production traffic analysis showed intermittent tail latency spikes and unfair queueing when many short requests contend with a small number of long-sequence requests. This PR tunes the continuous-batcher scheduler to provide stronger queueing fairness, explicit starvation prevention for low-latency paths, and adaptive per-request timeouts that reduce wasted waiting.

Goals: reduce 99th-percentile latency for short requests under mixed workloads, avoid starvation of low-priority/short jobs, and provide config knobs for controlled rollout.

Approach summary: (1) introduce a hierarchical queueing policy that splits incoming requests into latency bins (short/medium/long) based on sequence-length hint and recent token-rate estimates; (2) implement a dynamic fairness token allocator that ensures short-bin requests receive a minimum dispatch share while still allowing batching of long requests; (3) add a starvation-prevention path that forces dispatch of a pending request if it has waited beyond a configurable threshold; (4) add adaptive timeouts: batch wait_timeouts are computed per-bin using EWMA of dispatch latency and current queue depth instead of a fixed global timeout; (5) surface new metrics and config flags for canary rollouts.

Compatibility: default behavior is identical to previous scheduler when all new config flags are off. The new logic is guarded by runtime flags and a safe rollout path (canary percentage and per-cluster opt-in).

Testing: unit tests for queue partitioning and token allocator, integration tests that simulate mixed short/long request workloads, and an e2e perf canary compared to baseline under synthetic load. Local microbenchmarks show a 30-45% reduction in p99 latency for short requests in mixed workloads, with <=3% change in average throughput.

Rollout plan: land behind feature flag; enable on 10% of capacity for 24h with enhanced tracing; incrementally increase to 100% if no regressions.

Notes: this PR touches scheduler logic only; runtime kernel selection and KV-cache behavior are unchanged but future follow-ups will use the introduced bins to influence kernel and KV-cache allocation policies.

review_comments: Ava Martinez (reviewer): Can we get a short explanation for how bin thresholds are chosen? Are they purely sequence-length based or do you use tokens-per-second estimates?

Liam Chen (author): Thresholds default to sequence-length buckets but we compute an EWMA tokens/sec per-client to correct assignments for bursty short-but-high-token-rate requests. Added explanation and a note to docs.
